Applying the HC at Minerva
When creating any work, this HC will help you think deliberately about the field-specific professional norms and help you decide whether or not you should follow those norms.

Some examples of applications include:

When writing a paper, it is essential to check assignment instructions carefully and format your paper by referring to a style guide that matches the instructions. Beyond this, you should also consider formatting, style, and conventions that you’ve observed in the context of other written work you’ve studied for that class. Each discipline has its own norms, and being attentive to them will help you tailor your work to the nuanced expectations of each professional environment. Deviations from formatting requirements should be discussed with your instructor and justified in the HC footnote.
When delivering a presentation, whether live or recorded, you should use #audience to help you research the professional expectations of your audience and then tailor things like your background, attire, props, use of slides, etc. to that professional environment. For assignments in which you are teaching a class, or a section of a class, pay close attention to lesson plan formatting guidelines.
Under this HC, Minerva students learn what being professional means for our context at Minerva. As you’ve seen in this handbook, this includes footnoting, following assignment instructions, citing sources appropriately, showing up to class ready to engage and participate, behaving according to certain guidelines, etc. These norms are important to set community expectations. However, if a particular instance arose where a student wanted to explain why they did not follow specific guidelines for an assignment, or behaved a certain way in class, and grounded it in ideas about different norms for the given audience, that would be a very welcome application!
Showcasing deliberate style and formatting choices makes for a good application of this HC. Here are some footnote snippets that demonstrate non-trivial thought toward presentation:
I opted for a narrower spacing than conventional APA to prevent the document from being too many pages long, and ensure that my figure/table titles and captions fit on the same page as the corresponding element. Plus, single-spacing is commonly used in other formatting conventions and usually followed in published technical research papers.
In my appendix, I used a Google Doc extension that makes code look more like it was written in a code editor. By using a monospace font with different colors for different syntaxes, like keywords, variables, and comments, I made the code more readable and reflective of the correct indentation.
I used a Latex compiler instead of a generic text editor like Google Docs to format equations professionally. This helped me better align expressions in multi-line calculations.
Applying the HC Outside of Minerva
We regularly apply #professionalism when we adapt to subtle and often unspoken norms about how we interact with others in varied professional contexts. When you attend an awards ceremony, how you dress and what kinds of things you say in acceptance speeches depends on the professional context you’re entering. If you’re attending the Grammys, professionalism may look like stepping out of your comfort zone with a bold and stylish outfit and graciously supporting Grammy winners whether or not you agree with their merit. However, professional norms could be quite the opposite in a political debate. Professionalism may look like blending in with a plain suit, but standing out by voicing your opposing views in heated debate.

Sometimes, professional groups take pride in avoiding traditional professional norms. For example, you will likely see people in highly casual clothes at an evolutionary biology conference. Casual dress is a field-specific norm of such conferences. If one did not research what is considered professional, they might show up in a conventionally formal suit and tie, making themselves look uneducated and unprepared. Therefore, researching field-specific norms and avoiding assumptions about professionalism is always recommended.

Professionalism is commonly perceived as the practice of exhibiting responsibility, integrity, accountability, and excellence within a professional setting. This encompasses the utilization of suitable language, tone, and attire, as well as presenting oneself and one's work in a competent and ethical manner. However, a critical examination of the established norms of professionalism is imperative. For example, if working with an American organization, it’s likely that norms are predominantly formulated by individuals steeped in Western culture, thereby reflecting a white, Western-centric worldview.

Without deliberate instruction and contemplation on the origins of these standards, following them may inadvertently perpetuate a Western-centric cultural and social code. In some cases, this could create an unsafe or discriminatory environment for certain individuals if not addressed. It is vital to acknowledge and appreciate the diverse professional customs across different cultures and foster an understanding that professionalism can embody a spectrum of behaviors and practices, mirroring the diversity of an organization’s individuals and their global cultures.

Van Halen and M&Ms: When Van Halen was touring, they were famous for the detailed contract they would sign with venues where they performed. One specific element of the contract was that their dressing room had to be furnished with a bowl of M&Ms, with all of the brown ones removed. If the venue did not comply with the request, they would forfeit their payment for the show. People typically interpreted this as a random prima-donna rock-star power move. However, they had a specific reason for including this requirement in their contracts.

Van Halen’s shows involved a lot of pyrotechnics and elaborate electrical equipment. Other parts of the contract included details about wiring and positioning of various equipment. It was critically important for all of those instructions to be precisely followed. The problem is, a lot of that stuff is hard to check. You would have to look very closely at every single wire to make sure it was the appropriate gauge. Whether or not there are brown M&Ms in the dressing room is not important at all, but it is easy to check. The bowl of M&Ms served as a proxy, telling the band whether or not the venue had read the contract carefully and taken it seriously. If there were M&Ms in the dressing room with the brown ones removed, they felt they could trust that the stage had been set up correctly. If not, they knew they should go out and double check everything before the show.

Spelling and grammar are the brown M&Ms of a scientific paper. Every paper makes claims about the procedures they followed – how they collected and analyzed the data. It is very difficult, often impossible, for the reader to verify those claims. When the authors say they put 10mL of solution into each tube, how do we know they did not put in 9 or 11? Did they really incubate the culture for 30 minutes at 25 degrees? Was their thermometer calibrated? Did they remove it exactly when they were supposed to? Or was it 32 minutes at 26 degrees?

We can not independently verify many of a paper’s claims. However, we can see whether or not they paid attention to details like punctuation and formatting. If your writing shows a high degree of attention to all of the fine details, the reader is more likely to believe that you applied that same level of attention to detail to the science itself.

Identify and classify the relevant variables of a system, problem, or model.  Defining the HC icon Defining the HC

Pitch
Variables change. Before addressing how and why, we need to know what those variables are.

Paragraph Description
An important initial step in analyzing a problem, model, or system, is to evaluate the relevant variables: the features that can change. To do so, one must identify and classify the relevant variables, examine the relationships between them, and consider how they can be measured and manipulated. In the context of a study or experiment, this typically involves identifying which features play the role of independent variables, the hypothesized predictors, and which play the role of the dependent variable, the hypothesized response that results from changes in the independent variable(s). One may also need to identify confounding variables that could impact the relationship under study, and carefully consider how to mitigate their effects. Further, classifying the type of variables (for example, qualitative or quantitative) is essential as it will affect the type of statistical analyses that are appropriate. Representing a problem formally may also involve identifying the quantities that are constant (not varying), usually referred to as parameters. Parameters help to define the nature of the problem and can be treated as constraints on the solution.

Categorization
Habit of Mind | Formal Analyses | Thinking Critically | Analyzing Problems

Cornerstone Introduction
Class: Formal Analyses | Semester One

Unit: Problem Solving

Big Question: What does it mean to be random? How can data help us discover what is true?


General Example
You are working for the customer service department of a restaurant chain, and are interested in determining the degree to which server friendliness (the independent variable) can be used to predict tip percentage (the dependent variable). You hypothesize the following causal relationship between variables: you expect that friendly attendants will lead to satisfied customers, and that satisfied customers will provide a larger tip. This is supported by your previous research findings that people in a positive mood tend to be less stingy. You’re aware of several other extraneous variables that could affect tip percentages such as food quality, customer income, type of meal ordered, and time of day. This leads you to consider methods to diminish the effects of these variables on your results, attempting to control for them as much as possible. You also classify what type of variables these are, noting that server friendliness is usually ranked on an ordinal scale, which would change the type of statistical analyses performed on the collected data, leading you to suggest alternative ways to measure friendliness on the customer survey. Identifying and classifying these variables is your first step in formally representing the problem of interest which can now be further developed.

Footnote: As a first step for investigating the connection between service and tipping, the different variables are identified, classified, and the relationship between them is suggested. The variable types and roles inform the potential analysis that would be required and facilitates careful thought on the variables' measurement.

Common Pitfalls
The application identifies 'factors' in a system but does not formalize the factors by specifying how these factors vary or change, how they can be measured, or how they are related to each other.
The application confuses ordinal variables (e.g., star ratings) with quantitative variables.
The application does not define the units of measurement clearly or does so inconsistently. For example, the application introduces a variable in kilograms and later references the variable in pounds.
The application does not accurately distinguish between variables and parameters.
The application does not provide sufficient consideration or justification for the type of variables.
The application does not sufficiently explain the context around the variable: how it was measured, how it should be interpreted, and what its units are.
The application assumes a cause-effect relationship between the dependent and independent variables, while in reality, the dependent variable may not be a direct effect of independent variables.
The application uses inappropriate statistical techniques for the given variables. For example, a student may use Pearson’s correlation for an ordinal variable, while Spearman’s correlation or rank-based correlation measures would be more suitable.

As explained in the Minerva variables guide, one must have a solid foundation in #variables in order to correctly apply #hypothesisdevelopment, #modeling, #dataviz, #descriptivestats, #correlation, #significance, and more!

For example, when modeling the SIR model in Formal Analyses class, relevant variables and parameters must be defined, classified, and analyzed before diving into deriving the implications of the model.
In some NS and SS classes, applying #variables is useful to design or critique research studies, including experiments, interviews, and surveys.
Setting up an experiment to test the desired relationship or hypothesis requires a clear idea of what variables are independent and dependent. Further, identifying the control and confounding variables helps to make sure you consider how to set up your experiment properly to isolate the relationship of interest.
When it comes to designing surveys and interviews, the type of questions posed should depend on what you want to learn from the survey and what analysis you will perform on the collected data. If one wants to perform calculations to analyze the data, it's important to have quantitative variables. Qualitative variables can still be informative but need to be analyzed and interpreted with care.
In the physical sciences, identifying variables as 'vector' quantities or 'scalar' quantities is an important part of understanding that quantity. For example, speed is a scalar quantity, while velocity is a vector quantity. Vector quantities are defined by both a magnitude (e.g., 5 m/s) and a direction (e.g., east). This distinction is important because vector quantities require different treatment than scalar quantities, usually involving geometry and trigonometry.
Dimensional analysis is important across NS, so it’s crucial to understand the dimensions of relevant quantities. Relatedly, it’s also important to consider the most appropriate units for each quantity under study.
In business courses that require spreadsheet analysis with several variables, it’s important to consider the variable types to select appropriate correlational analyses.
Applying the HC Outside of Minerva
This HC is applicable to different fields in NS and CS. For example, if you are a Machine Learning developer you will have to consider the relevant variables and their types when creating different models (e.g. regression analysis). Such models are now the backbone of various services, such as Netflix, Tiktok, and YouTube’s recommendation algorithms.
Studying any complex system, whether it be social, physical, or economic, requires understanding and representing many interacting agents. This includes a huge variety of systems from physics, to transportation, the weather, communication networks, and many more. The application of #variables is essential to ensure the characterization of all agents is appropriately modeled.

Identify and apply constraint satisfaction as a way to solve problems. Defining the HC icon Defining the HC

Pitch
While constraints limit solutions, they can be catalysts for the solution-finding process.

Paragraph Description
A problem exists when one or more obstacles to a goal must be addressed. Obstacles often cannot be overcome easily, largely because there are constraints on what actions are possible or realistic. Constraints are requirements for the solution; they do not determine it but place boundaries on what is possible. Thus, part of solving a problem is identifying the constraints on what can be done. If the constraints are well-defined, problems can often be solved by devising ways to satisfy all of the constraints simultaneously. This approach to problem solving is known as “constraint satisfaction.”

Categorization
Foundational Concept | Empirical Analyses | Thinking Creatively | Solving Problems

Cornerstone Introduction
Class: Empirical Analyses | Semester One

Unit: Problem Solving

Big Question: How can we feed the world?


General Example
You are moving into a new house and need to decide where to put the furniture in your bedroom. You have an old sofa that is missing a rear leg and sits on a telephone book, so you don’t want to put it in a location where it can be seen from behind. You realize, however, there is no place to put the sofa so that it is not seen from behind, and so you decide to treat this as an obstacle rather than a constraint and get the sofa fixed. You budget so that you spend less money on groceries this week so you have enough money to overcome the obstacle: in other words, fix the sofa. You also have an old bed, with a headboard that must lean against the wall. Fixing the headboard would cost way more than fixing the sofa, so it is not feasible, and you decide to keep it as a constraint to be satisfied. Additionally, you have two end tables, which must be set to either side of the headboard. And a large chair and reading lamp, which must be near each other. Once you pick a wall for the headboard (one of the constraints), the positions of the other pieces of furniture may be determined. There is only one other place where the wall can accommodate the headboard, and once it and the end tables are set up, there is only one other place large enough for the chair and lamp. Because you fixed the sofa, you can put it anywhere where space is left. The mere act of satisfying all of the constraints and overcoming obstacles simultaneously almost dictates the solution to the problem.

Footnote: Upon facing numerous alternative choices to place furniture, the constraints that must be satisfied by a solution are identified and fulfilled sequentially to guide the furniture arrangement; in this case, satisfying all the constraints directly solved the problem.

Applying the HC at Minerva
You’re a junior with an NS major. When you’re selecting courses for the lottery, you may impose several constraints, such as:

Out of all the possible combinations of courses offered in the semester, you reduced many options just by trying to satisfy the constraints above. This method greatly simplified the decision making process.

In physics, there are physical laws that constrain the relationship between dynamical quantities. Using these laws as constraints helps one to characterize the motion of an object or system. For example, for an oscillating pendulum under simple harmonic motion, the law of conservation of energy guarantees that the total mechanical energy (kinetic energy + potential energy) is constant at all times. This conservation law can be translated into a mathematical equation that serves as a constraint on the system, specifying the relationship between mass, speed, and position. Using this constraint allows one to fully evaluate the motion of the pendulum. For example, its speed at a given position can be determined. There are other conservation laws too, such as the conservation of momentum and the conservation of linear momentum. Being able to recognize scenarios in which these laws apply can be a powerful problem solving tool!
Applying the HC Outside of Minerva
Flight search engines, such as Google Flights, Skiplagged, and Skyscanner, are built on the principles of constrained optimization. For example, if you’re flying from Taipei to Buenos Aires (which is usually challenging, here’s a video explaining why), you can input several filters, such as:
The budget range
The maximum number of transits
Airlines offering a carbon offset option
The minimum baggage allowance
Duration of flight(s)
Date(s) of departure
These filters act as constraints, thus reducing the number of possible routes to travel from these two cities. The options listed for you are all viable solutions that satisfy your constraints.

Defining the HC icon Defining the HC

Pitch
If you’re not carefully characterizing your problem, you ARE the problem.

Paragraph Description
The first step to solving a problem is to characterize exactly what the problem is. This helps to ensure that proposed solutions address the right problem—the one that needs to be solved. Characterizing a problem requires specifying the initial and goal states, the obstacles that stand between the starting situation and the goals, and the scale of the problem. Different types of solutions are appropriate for problems that arise at different scales.

Categorization
Habit of Mind | Empirical Analyses | Thinking Creatively | Analyzing Problems

Cornerstone Introduction
Class: Empirical Analyses | Semester One

Unit: Problem Solving

Big Question: How can we feed the world?


General Example
Events that ensure interaction between students and their rotation cities are at the heart of the Minerva experience. During the COVID-19 pandemic, these events were unable to happen as they originally did, as measures of social distancing and quarantine were in effect and many students studied remotely. Aiming to still promote student engagement and interactions, understanding the core problem was key to designing appropriate solutions. The initial state of the problem was that original in-city Minerva programs were canceled and students were at risk of feeling disconnected from their community. While some students were in rotation cities, a large percentage were totally remote. The goal state was for all students to have opportunities to engage with their class, feel a sense of belonging, and connect their academic experience to their student life experience. The scale of the problem concerned the whole Minerva community, internationally, though considering the problem at the cohort scale also seemed useful. The most relevant obstacles included (1) fearful mindsets about the pandemic, (2) the pandemic added uncertainty to planning, and (3) student routines and needs changed.

Footnote: This application of #rightproblem consists of a problem-focused analysis, that starts with some general context but then narrows down to the problem characterization of initial state, goal state, scale and obstacles. It is important that this stage of problem solving is focused on understanding the depth and scope of a complex problem we want to solve, and ideation and selection of solutions will come up later on in the process. Ways this characterization could've been stronger include quantifying information about the scenario and including more aspects than just disconnect and lack of interaction (for example, the mental health impacts of the pandemic).
